text: I think your point about the inevitability of the passage of time is the biggest element of this. New artists are coming out, releasing their first records every single day, and then they keep releasing new stuff after that. Even if we don't account for the ways in which tastes change over time, the fact that there are new releases every day means that, by necessity, people are going to have less time to explore the artists from long ago. We've been recording music in some capacity for about a hundred years at this point, and every year along that timeline has had more recorded music than the year before. Of COURSE people are going to be listening to older artists less. Before you complain about "kids these days" not liking artists from the 80s or the 70s or even the 50s, ask yourself how much stuff you were listening to from the 20s or 30s when you were their age.

text: I would even go further back than that to say that before physical recording media, music was reproduced and disseminated via notation. I'm still discovering new [to me] things to love written three centuries ago by J.S. Bach. I agree that each generation is relatively myopic when it comes to ideas from the past. I also feel like the acts that are preserved and carried forward aren't always the most seemingly memorable purely based on merit. Other factors influence who is remembered and forgotten, including changing cultural values, but also patronage, affiliation, utility, ownership of IP, profitability, resurgence and rediscovery, etc.

text: It's not so much "kids these days", but I think comparing eras that way can be tricky. Like, the recordings of the 20s and 30s just aren't very good. The music may be interesting but the technology just wasn't there. It wasn't until the west got the magnetic tape tech from the nazis after WWII that recordings started to sound really good. And then you had guys like Les Paul doing crazy things with layering and overdubbing and then with the advent of stereo recording, and later quadrophonic and upwards, it's like going from black and white to color TV. And I think that was the time music recording "matured". That 1967 to about 1977ish time period was the peak of analog music recording and high fidelity. And many of those recordings still hold up after 60 years regardless of genre, while the same can't be said for something like Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music (released in the 50s, but was recorded through the 20s and 30s). You can go from Pink Floyd to Earth Wind & Fire to Stevie Wonder to Caravan to Peter Tosh to whoever, and the recordings generally all sound fantastic from that time.
label: substantive

text: # "batch_3" (thread: The debate between band performing live and using backing tracks)

For small gigs if I notice a backing track I'm leaving (I include loopers in this). For bigger stuff I begrudingly accept that I'm paying more for a "show" than a concert and accept there will probably be backing tracks. But if it's a show known for excessive usage of tracks I just won't buy a ticket. Lip syncing is never ok under any circumstances.
label: substantive

text: It's less a matter of "debate" and more a matter of necessity in a live environment. Every single professional touring act has backing tracks to some degree. Backing tracks are not just for pantomiming to or adding parts that were multitracked without hiring more performers. Two big ones are to provide monitor mixes and to act as failovers if someone has a malfunction that takes more than a few seconds to resolve. The performers will record those tracks during rehearsals or use previous live performances to make it pretty seamless live. Again, these can be laced in with an actual live feed pretty easily and on the fly for each member of the band. They're pretty crucial and are used way more than most people will ever know.
label: substantive

text: "Every single professional touring act has backing tracks to some degree." This is wildly untrue, and highly genre dependent. It may be true for modern rock and pop acts, but in bluegrass, for example, getting caught using a backing track would be a career ending scandal.

text: Ah... the great bassist drought of the 2020s! In the 1990s I had a strictly improv ambient echo loop act (it was generally a one-person act but a violinist friend, lap steel guitarist, and percussionist pal sometimes joined me for special performances at festivals and such - under a different name). At the time I was also playing acoustic solo, folkie sets - as well as recording 'produced' multitrack versions of those songs in a defiantly non-commercial array of styles. It did occur to me to me that I could take my little laptop, run a MIDI sequence from its floppy drive, and maybe people would be impressed with 'the full package.' But I rolled it around in my mind a lot, thought about acts I had seen in the past that used pre-sequenced pre-programmed music and just decided I didn't really want to go there. I'd rather play live, spontaneous music than play records for an audience. (Now, there is a certain art to spinning DJ platters, and I've done that, stepping in for others on occasion; it's fun - and challenging trying to keep the dance floor filled. But it's really nothing like playing music to my way of thinking. The son of one of my friends - and old band mates - is a pretty successful electronica DJ. Since it seemed kind of parallel to my own ambient echo loop act, I was hoping to enjoy it more, but I can't really say that I did. No shade on the fine young man and his fervent following, but it was all samples and pre-programmed sequences. There seemed nothing spontaneous about it.) I'm sure it's very exciting to see thousands (or tens of thousands) of party goers responding to the show, but it captured none of the excitement I feel when I watch a symphony, a good jazz performance, or some folky singing his heart out.
